Lamentable
LAM-en-tuh-bul
adj. (mournful; of the voice Darius used at the mouth of the lions' den)
From Latin lamentabilis, from lamentari, to wail. At Daniel 6:20 it renders an Aramaic word meaning grieved or pained — the king's voice after a sleepless night.

Biblical Definition

Darius has been manoeuvred by his own princes into signing a decree he could not revoke, and has spent the night fasting, refusing music, unable to sleep. At first light he runs to the den: And when he came to the den, he cried with a lamentable voice unto Daniel: and the king spake and said to Daniel, O Daniel, servant of the living God, is thy God, whom thou servest continually, able to deliver thee from the lions? It is one of the most affecting moments in the Old Testament — the most powerful man in the world shouting into a pit, hoping.

Two details in the king's own words repay attention. He calls Daniel servant of the living God, a confession from a pagan monarch, and he had already said the night before, Thy God whom thou servest continually, he will deliver thee. What made Darius say that was not theology but a lifetime of watching one man's habits. Daniel's enemies had counted on the same thing — they framed the decree precisely because they knew he would pray three times a day with his windows open toward Jerusalem, and that he would not stop. And the answer that comes up out of the dark is as calm as the king's voice is not: My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): to be lamented; mournful; expressing sorrow; sorrowful.

expand to see more

LAMENTABLE, a. To be lamented; mournful; adapted to awaken grief; expressing sorrow.

LAMENT, v.i. To mourn; to weep or wail; to express sorrow.

DEN, n. A cave or hollow place in the earth; a cavern used as a lair by wild beasts.

DECREE, n. Judicial decision, or determination of a litigated cause; an edict or law made by a superior authority.

INNOCENCY, n. Freedom from guilt; harmlessness; simplicity of heart.

Key Scripture

Daniel 6:20 — "And when he came to the den, he cried with a lamentable voice unto Daniel: and the king spake and said to Daniel, O Daniel, servant of the living God, is thy God, whom thou servest continually, able to deliver thee from the lions?"

Daniel 6:16 — "Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions. Now the king spake and said unto Daniel, Thy God whom thou servest continually, he will deliver thee."

Daniel 6:22 — "My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me: forasmuch as before him innocency was found in me; and also before thee, O king, have I done no hurt."

Ecclesiastes 7:2 — "It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart."

Modern Corruption

Daniel 6 is filed as a children's story, and the adult point — that a law was written specifically to make faithfulness illegal, and a man kept his windows open — is lost.

expand to see more

The lions' den survives in most memories as a picture book, and the actual mechanism of the chapter is forgotten. Daniel's enemies could find no fault in his administration, so they concluded, in so many words, that they would find occasion against him concerning the law of his God. They then drafted a thirty-day statute, formally lawful, that made his ordinary devotion a capital offence. Daniel did not protest the decree, did not organize, and did not hide: he went into his house, his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day... as he did aforetime. The phrase as he did aforetime is the whole of it. He changed nothing.

The other half is Darius, and he is a warning to any man with authority. He was not malicious; he was flattered, hurried, and trapped by his own signature, and he spent the night paying for it. A ruler who signs what is put in front of him because it honours him will find himself shouting into a pit at daybreak. And the pagan king's lamentable voice asking whether the living God is able is answered by the quiet voice from the dark — which is how Scripture usually arranges these things.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Aramaic atsib (H6088), grieved, pained; gob (H1358), a den or pit; shezib (H7804), to deliver.

expand to see more

Aramaic atsib (H6088) — grieved, pained; the adjective on the king's voice.

Aramaic gob (H1358) — a den, a pit; where Daniel spent the night.

Aramaic shezib (H7804) — to rescue, to deliver; used repeatedly in the chapter of what God can do.

Aramaic chay (H2417) — living; servant of the living God, from a pagan king's mouth.

Aramaic zakku (H2136) — innocency, purity; found in Daniel before God and before the king.

Usage

"“he cried with a lamentable voice unto Daniel” — the most powerful man in the world, shouting into a pit."

"“Thy God whom thou servest continually” — a pagan's testimony to a lifetime of habit."

"“My God hath sent his angel” — the answer from the dark."
